articles.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 - API Pricing & Benchmarks
articles.text:
Different companies host the same model. OpenRouter routes your request to one of them based on the routing mode you pick — Balanced (price + speed), Nitro (fastest), or Floor (cheapest).

The average price customers actually pay for this model, next to the prices providers post. Caching and discounts mean the price actually paid is often well below the listed one.

Throughput is how fast the model writes (tokens per second — higher is better). Latency is total round-trip time (lower is better). TTFT is time-to-first-token — how long before you see anything appear (lower is better).

Uptime is the percentage of the past 3 days that at least one provider was responding to requests. Availability is the percentage of time that inference was successfully served. OpenRouter continuously monitors and uses the next-best provider when one returns an error.

Scores on standardized evaluations and this model’s own outputs on shared benchmark prompts. Higher percentages are better — and each rank shows where this model lands among the models evaluated on that source.

articles.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins \ Anthropic
articles.text:
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.
ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information on where it came from.Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:	“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”Jerry Solinas, 2015Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.Claude found the seedsSeveral Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1,842 iterations to output the standardized seed.What this meansThis is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.How it was foundSearches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state. Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5,810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.Claude found some base points tooBut wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3, and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP, Arjen Lenstra's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup's NTL library shipped the same code.The recipe here is simple:Seed the generator with a small integer.Throw away seven outputs.Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507, and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.Open questionsNot every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve, and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1,842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.The bountyThe $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group.Who we areThis work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.AcknowledgmentsWe would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “evil Internet meme” and the “Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen” with good humor. Also thanks to Filippo Valsorda for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.Code to reproduce the seedsfrom datetime import datetime, timezone

def unix(when):
return int(datetime.fromisoformat(when).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).timestamp())

def candidate(t, n, per, shift, width):
x, out = (t << 16) | 0x330E, ""                      # the state srand48(t) sets
for i in range(per * n):
x = (0x5DEECE66D * x + 0xB) % 2**48              # one step of lrand48
if i >= per * (n - 1):
out += "%0*X" % (width, x >> shift)
return out

PRIME = {  # srand48(time); 20 bytes per candidate: lrand48() >> 23
"prime239v1": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2185),
"prime239v2": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2320),
"prime239v3": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 3048),
"P-192":      ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 139),
"prime192v3": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 5228),
"prime192v2": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 6013),
"P-521":      ("1997-08-08 01:12:04", 1136),
"P-256":      ("1997-08-16 01:52:34", 1842),
"P-384":      ("1997-08-30 14:50:08", 2688),
"P-224":      ("1998-04-03 12:52:07", 7026),
}
BINARY = {  # srand48(time / 2), if that reading is right; 5 words per candidate: lrand48()
"B-233": ("1998-04-17 15:24:18", 155),
"B-283": ("1998-04-17 15:27:44", 32),
"B-409": ("1998-04-17 15:30:18", 60),
"B-571": ("1998-04-17 15:32:08", 73),
}
for name, (when, n) in PRIME.items():
print(f"{name:10} {when} {n:5} {candidate(unix(when), n, 20, 40, 2)}")
for name, (when, n) in BINARY.items():
print(f"{name:10} {when} {n:5} {candidate(unix(when) // 2, n, 5, 17, 8)}")

articles.sourceTitle: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
articles.title: A benchmark map of the US economy
articles.text:
A benchmark map
of the US economyThe Benchmark MapEach tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks.All 22 job familiesclick a family to open itCoverage byCovered with at leastBenchmark IndexNo coverageIn our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts, and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations.Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks. This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage billHigh AI exposureLow AI exposureAdjusted probability of task coverage0%5%10%15%20%High AI exposureLow AI exposure$500m$1bn$2bn$5bn$10bn$20bn$50bnAnnualized occupation wage bill (log scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.Methodology in briefTo break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations.Example — 6 of the 22 tasks O*NET associates with Lawyers1Prepare, draft, and review legal documents, such as wills, deeds, patent applications, mortgages, leases, and contracts.2Advise clients concerning business transactions, claim liability, advisability of prosecuting or defending lawsuits, or legal rights and obligations.3Interpret laws, rulings and regulations for individuals and businesses.4Analyze the probable outcomes of cases, using knowledge of legal precedents.5Present evidence to defend clients or prosecute defendants in criminal or civil litigation.6Supervise legal assistants.To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:Public Availability. Included benchmarks have at least 25 publicly available tasks. We also include Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, where we have access to held-out benchmark prompts and are therefore able to map them to O*NET tasks.Agentic Tasks. Included benchmarks ask models to perform agentic tasks, rather than answering questions or advising the user on how to complete a task.Economic Realism. Benchmark tasks resemble tasks which humans (or agents) are frequently asked to do in real-world enterprises. Economically valuable tasks are prioritized over academically complex ones.Economic Diversity. We capped the number of included benchmarks per job family, in significant part to account for the massive overrepresentation of software engineering and research tasks in popular benchmarks.Balanced Difficulty. Benchmarks are not yet saturated by frontier models.Following work by Wang et al., we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al.’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab.LimitationsOur estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.Patterns in coverageThe benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al.), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation.But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts:Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage billHigh AI exposureLow AI exposureAdjusted probability of task coverage0%5%10%15%20%High AI exposureLow AI exposure$500m$1bn$2bn$5bn$10bn$20bn$50bnAnnualized occupation wage bill (log scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important:Benchmark coverage by O*NET task importance within occupationsHigh AI exposureLow AI exposureAdjusted probability of task coverage0%5%10%15%20%High AI exposureLow AI exposure3.253.503.754.004.254.504.75O*NET task importance (1–5 rating scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that, controlling for occupation, an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag and a given quintile O*NET importance score is covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Importance quintiles are calculated from O*NET importance scores. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and importance quintiles, with occupation fixed effects. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.The plots above suggest a reasonable allocation of the relatively limited resources devoted to high-quality, economically relevant benchmarks so far; it’s natural to prioritize making benchmarks which cover the most important and AI-exposed tasks in the occupations with the largest wage bills. But barring a significant increase in the number and diversity of such benchmarks, these patterns will result in significant blind spots in our view of economically valuable model capabilities.Can O*NET + benchmarks tell us how good AI is at your job?Measuring model capabilities by job occupation is essential – for enterprises deciding which models fit their needs, for policymakers forecasting the economic impact of AI, and for Americans thinking about their careers. Unfortunately, this is a hard problem to solve.We could just try averaging model performance on all benchmark prompts relevant to a given job. But as our Benchmark Map suggests, benchmarks cover some economic tasks much more intensively than others. A simple average would give too much weight to frequently benchmarked tasks.O*NET offers a way to potentially reduce this bias. If we average model performance on occupation-relevant benchmark prompts weighted by O*NET classification, so that each O*NET task is equally weighted in our occupation average, we get a step closer to a number that represents real economic performance.As a first step, we try this approach on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks for four occupations: investment banking, law, accounting, and software engineering. We compare O*NET-weighted scores to simple averages of model performance on tasks related to each occupation. The resulting weighted and unweighted scores are generally quite similar:APEX-1 + APEX-Agents · O*NET: Financial and Investment Analysts · 11 tasks · 176 promptsScore (%)Every prompt counts equallyEvery O*NET task counts equallyClaude Fable 5.1 Max69.8%68.5%Claude Opus 5.5 Max73.3%70.2%Claude Opus 5 Max65.5%63.0%GPT-6 Astra Max65.5%61.8%GPT-5.6 Sol Max66.8%65.6%Grok 4.7 xHigh58.1%58.7%Gemini 3.8 Flash High66.9%67.5%Kimi K3 Max59.4%59.9%DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Max56.5%58.4%Claude Fable 5.1 MaxClaude Opus 5.5 MaxClaude Opus 5 MaxGPT-6 Astra MaxGPT-5.6 Sol MaxGrok 4.7 xHighGemini 3.8 Flash HighKimi K3 MaxDeepSeek V4.1 Flash Max10%20%30%40%50%60%70%80%90%Score (%)For each oc

articles.sourceTitle: How the Claude Code team does code review
articles.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
articles.text:
We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?
This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.
We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.
RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW
When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.
Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.
Code review does two jobs:

Find and fix issues before they ship
Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"
Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.
Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.
THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION
We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.
Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.
So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.
THE LIFE OF A CHANGE
A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.

1. The work is verified before anyone else looks
Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.
Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.
Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."
When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.
REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

2. AI review on every pull request
Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?
On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.
When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.
Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.
Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.
3. Security review that can block
Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.
If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code.
4. Automated checks that block
The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.
5. Human approval, scaled by risk
A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.
RiskExamplesHuman approvalsLowDocs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flagNone required once automated review and security checks are greenMediumOrdinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system promptsOne personHighThe highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two peopleTwo people
The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.
Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.
Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.
An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.
6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release
The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it.
7. Fast detection, fast rollback
Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flag

articles.sourceTitle: You could have invented transformers from memory
articles.title: You could have invented transformers from memory
articles.text:
Retrieving a character from memory. The recall worsens as the number of memories grows.Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world.
Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium.
It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again.
We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to.
The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity.We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory.An outer product memory store#The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,$$W = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i k_i\transpose = V\transpose K$$where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$.1To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights.2Aside: a gradient descent step writes a memoryTake a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer’s output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, so a step with learning rate $\eta$ is$$W \leftarrow W - \eta\, \bar y x\transpose.$$This recurrence is a memory update: it updates the weights with a new memory with key $x$ and value $-\eta\bar y$.
For more on this view, see Irie, Csordás & Schmidhuber, who express a linear layer trained by gradient descent as attention over all of its training inputs.To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:$$f(x) = V\transpose K x = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,(k_i\transpose x).$$So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.Recall picks up interference#So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?Let’s assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then$$f(k_j) = \underbrace{v_j}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq j} v_i\,(k_i\transpose k_j)}_{\text{interference}},$$meaning we get back the value of the target memory, the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.What is the outer-product store’s capacity? Here’s an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference’s squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal’s, and$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \sim \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k}}.$$Setting this ratio to 1 gives a capacity of$$M \approx d_k,$$once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.Each bar below is one stored memory’s weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory’s weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we’ll build later in the post.stored memories M = 32

sharpness β = 8

recall failsHow do we reduce interference?#Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall.3 To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to reduce interference.The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store’s capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more selectively: every memory in a linear store contributes interference, even when its key has low similarity to the query, so we can improve recall by suppressing the less similar keys.In the rest of the post, we’ll see that storing outer product memories more carefully gives us the optimal linear memory store, which has about twice the capacity. Recalling selectively via nonlinearities gives us MLPs and self-attention.The optimal linear memory store#The outer-product store writes each memory without regard to the others. Instead, we can choose the weights $W$ so that recall fits all of the stored memories at once. This is a linear regression problem:4$$\operatorname*{minimize}_W \sum_{i=1}^M \norm{W k_i - v_i}_2^2.$$When we store more memories than the key dimension, $M > d_k$, the least-squares solution is$$W = \parens*{\sum_i v_i k_i\transpose}\parens*{\sum_i k_i k_i\transpose}\inverse = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse.$$This is the outer-product store $V\transpose K$ with one change: before we compare the query with the keys, we multiply it by $(K\transpose K)\inverse$, which undoes the keys’ covariance $K\transpose K$. This whitens the keys, so the store no longer overweights directions that many keys share.When $M \leq d_k$, the regression can fit every memory exactly, as long as the keys are linearly independent. So the optimal store recalls with no interference at all, even when the keys aren’t orthogonal.When $M > d_k$, we start to get interference, since there are only $d_k$ directions for the memory store to work with. For random keys and values, our interference-to-signal ratio becomes$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k} - 1}.$$This ratio equals 1 at$$M = 2d_k,$$so the optimal store’s capacity is twice as large as before!Aside: deriving the optimal linear memory storeWhen $M \leq d_k$. If the keys are linearly independent, the $M\times M$ matrix of inner products between keys, $KK\transpose$, is invertible, and$$W = V\transpose (KK\transpose)\inverse K$$fits every memory exactly. When $M < d_k$, the problem is underconstrained and has infinitely many solutions, and this one is the min-norm solution. The rows $\tilde k_i\transpose$ of $(KK\transpose)\inverse K$ are known as the dual basis for the rows of $K$: by construction, $(KK\transpose)\inverse KK\transpose = I$, so $\tilde k_i\transpose k_j = \delta_{ij}$. Then $f(k_j) = \sum_i v_i\, \tilde k_i\transpose k_j = v_j$, so there is no interference and we have perfect recall.When $M > d_k$. Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $W K\transpose K = V\transpose K$, so $W = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse$.
Both solutions are $W = V\transpose (K\transpose)\pinv$, where $A\pinv$ denotes the pseudoinverse of $A$: $(K\transpose)\pinv = (KK\transpose)\inverse K$ when the keys are linearly independent, and $(K\transpose)\pinv = K(K\transpose K)\inverse$ when they span $\reals^{d_k}$.Now we can analyze the interference of $f(k_j) = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$.
For a stored key $k_j$, the weight on each value $v_i$ is $k_i\transpose (K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$, which is exactly entry $(i, j)$ of the $M\times M$ matrix $P = K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose$:$$f(k_j) = \sum_{i=1}^M v_i\, P_{ij} = \underbrace{P_{jj}\, v_j}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq j} P_{ij}\, v_i}_{\text{interference}}.$$$P$ is the projection onto the column space of $K$, a $d_k$-dimensional subspace of $\reals^M$. Two facts about projections help us analyze the interference-to-signal ratio:The signal term: By the cyclic property of the trace,
$$\sum_{j=1}^M P_{jj} = \trace{K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose} = \trace{(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose K} = \trace{I_{d_k}} = d_k,$$
so the $M$ signal weights add up to $d_k$. If the keys are random, no key is special, so $P_{jj} \approx d_k/M$.The interference term: $P$ is a symmetric projection matrix, so $P\transpose P = P^2 = P$. Then
$$\sum_{i\neq j} P_{ij}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^M P_{ij}^2 - P_{jj}^2 = (P\transpose P)_{jj} - P_{jj}^2 = P_{jj} - P_{jj}^2 \approx \frac{d_k}{M} - \parens*{\frac{d_k}{M}}^2.$$If the values are random with similar lengths,$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \approx \frac{\sqrt{P_{jj} - P_{jj}^2}}{P_{jj}} = \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k} - 1}.$$Compared to the outer-product store’s $\sqrt{M/d_k}$, the $-1$ is the $d_k$ memories’ worth of interference that the optimal store cancels.We can check our predictions numerically. We randomly sample $M$ memories with unit-length keys in $d_k = 64$ dimensions, query the memory store with one of the stored keys, and measure the interference-to-signal ratio:recall fails: more interference than signal0.111016642561024409616384number of stored memories M (key dimension dk = 64)interference / signaloptimal: no interference for M ≤ 64outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 16: interference/signal = 0.46outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 32: interference/signal = 0.68outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 64: interference/signal = 0.97outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 128: interference/signal = 1.39outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 256: interference/signal = 1.97outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 512: interference/signal = 2.81outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 1024: interference/signal = 3.90outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 2048: interference/signal = 5.63outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 4096: interference/signal = 8.01outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 8192: interference/signal = 11.38outer-product (Hebbian) memory, M = 16384: interference/signal = 15.90outer productoptimal (least-squares) memory, M = 16: interference/signal = 0.00optimal (least-squares) memory, M = 32: interference/signal = 0.00optimal (least-squares) memory, M
